title: The Lowercase Subject Line Kit: Subject Lines That Look Sent by Mistake
description: How to write 1-3 word, lowercase subject lines that look like a coworker sent them. 40 examples, a test plan, mistakes to avoid and a copy-paste prompt.
lead: This is the full lowercase subject line kit from the reel. The best cold email subject lines look like they were sent by mistake: short, plain, lowercase, like a note from a coworker. Here's why that works, how to write them, 40 examples to start from and how to test them.
insider: Every campaign we run starts with plain, coworker-style copy and a subject line test on a small list before anything scales. For one agency client, that approach got a **3.19% reply rate, with 88% of replies positive**, every week for four and a half months. Writing the subject line takes a minute. The list, the inboxes and the follow-ups behind it are the system we run for clients.

blocks.text: Why "sent by mistake" works

Your buyer scans their inbox in a second or two. Their brain sorts every line into two piles: **people I know** and **companies selling to me**. Marketing emails have long, polished, Title Case subject lines with numbers and hype. Coworkers write things like "quick question" or "budget".

A short lowercase subject line lands in the first pile. It looks like a forwarded note, a reply or something a colleague typed fast. That's the "sent by mistake" feeling, and it's what earns the open.

blocks.label: The honest part
blocks.text: Lowercase alone is not magic. In [Belkins' study of 5.5 million emails](https://belkins.io/blog/b2b-cold-email-subject-line-statistics), lowercase and Title Case did about the same. What changed results was **length and tone**: short, plain and not salesy. Lowercase is just the easiest way to make a line look human.
What the data says

head: Finding
Source
rows: Subject lines of **2-4 words** got the highest open rate (46%). 10-word lines got 34%.
Belkins, 5.5M emails
Single-word subject lines got 38%. They can look automated or lack context.
Belkins, 5.5M emails
Hype, urgency ("ASAP") and generic greetings pushed open rates below 36%.
Belkins, 5.5M emails
Don't sell in the subject line. Avoid marketing language, buzzwords, numbers and questions.
Gong, 28M+ cold emails
Buzzwords and numbers reduce open rates by up to 17.9%.
Gong, 28M+ cold emails
Subject lines with two personal details got a 40.2% open rate vs 35.4% with one.
Hunter, 31M emails

blocks.text: So the target is clear: **1-3 plain words, lowercase, about them, no pitch.** The reel says 1-3 words. Belkins' sweet spot is 2-4. Treat 2-3 words as home base, and one word only when it's very specific (their company name, a project, a city).
The 5 rules

items: **1-3 words.** Phones cut subject lines after about 35 to 50 characters ([Belkins](https://belkins.io/blog/b2b-cold-email-subject-line-statistics)). Short lines show in full and look like a quick note.
**All lowercase.** No capital at the start, no Title Case. People typing fast to a colleague don't format. Keep real names normal if lowercase looks odd ("Acme" is fine).
**Boring on purpose.** Pick a word a coworker would use: "hiring", "next quarter", "your site". Boring looks internal. Clever looks like marketing.
**About them, not you.** Their company, their team, their project. Never your product name, never your offer.
**Match the first line.** The subject line opens the door. The first line has to explain it right away, or the open turns into a delete.

blocks.label: Use the generic ones less
blocks.text: "quick question" and "thought" are now used by thousands of senders. They still look human, but lines with a real detail about the person do better. Hunter found subject lines with two personal details got a **40.2% open rate vs 35.4%** with one.
Worked example: before and after

head: Before (looks like marketing)
After (looks sent by mistake)
rows: Boost Your Q4 Sales By 30% With AI-Powered Outreach!
q4 pipeline
Partnership Opportunity For Summit Dental
summit dental
Are You Struggling To Book Meetings?
empty calendar
🚀 Exclusive Offer: Free Lead Audit
your lead flow
Following Up On My Previous Email Regarding Our Services
following up

blocks.text: Here's a full email using the "after" style for a dental group that just opened a second location:

blocks.label: Example email
blocks.text:
Subject: new austin office

Hi Maria,

Saw Summit Dental opened the second office in Austin last month. Congrats.

New locations usually take a few months to fill the chair schedule. We help dental groups book new patient consults with simple email outreach to local employers.

Worth a quick look?

Sam
Notice the subject line makes no sense alone, and that's the point. It makes total sense the moment she reads the first line.
How to test it (without fooling yourself)

Judge subject lines by **replies, not opens**. Open tracking adds a hidden image to your email, and [Hunter's 2026 report](https://hunter.io/the-state-of-cold-email) found campaigns without open tracking got **7.4% replies vs 4.4%** with it. Many inboxes also load images on their own, so open numbers are unreliable anyway.

items: Write two subject lines for the same email: your current one (A) and a lowercase one (B). Change nothing else.
Split one list in two random halves of at least 200 people each.
Turn open tracking off. Send both on the same days, from the same inboxes.
Wait until the sequence finishes, then compare reply rates.
Keep the winner. Next round, test the winner against a new lowercase line.

blocks.text: **Example:** A goes to 200 people and gets 6 replies, a **3% reply rate**. B goes to the other 200 and gets 12 replies, a **6% reply rate**. B doubled the replies, so B becomes your new default. If the gap is only 1 or 2 replies, it's noise: test again on a bigger list before you decide.
Common mistakes

head: Mistake
Why it hurts
Fix
rows: Fake "re:" or "fwd:"
Pretends you talked before. People feel tricked and report spam.
Never fake a reply thread. Plain words do the same job honestly.
Subject has nothing to do with the email
Gets the open, then the delete. Feels like clickbait.
The first line must explain the subject right away.
Using the same line for everyone
Spam filters and tired buyers spot repeats.
Put one real detail in: company, city, project.
Sneaking the pitch back in
"free audit", "save 30%" look like marketing even in lowercase.
No offer, no numbers, no product name.
One word with no context
"hey" or "hi" looks automated. Belkins saw single words at 38% vs 46% for 2-4 words.
Use 2-3 words, or one very specific word.
Judging by open rate
Open tracking is unreliable and can lower replies.
Turn it off and judge by replies.

blocks.text: Write them with Claude or ChatGPT

blocks.label: Prompt
blocks.text:
You write cold email subject lines that look like a coworker sent them.

Prospect: [name], [job title] at [company].
What I know about them: [recent news, hiring, launch, post, location].
My email's first line: [paste it].

Write 10 subject lines.
Rules:
- 1 to 3 words, all lowercase
- plain, boring words a colleague would use
- about them, never about my product or offer
- no numbers, no emojis, no questions, no hype words, no fake "re:" or "fwd:"
- each one must make sense once the first line is read

Then pick the best 2 to A/B test and say why in one sentence each.

blocks.label: Quick check before you send
blocks.text: Read your subject line out loud and ask: would a coworker send this to me? If it sounds like an ad, cut words until it doesn't.

faq.q: Won't lowercase look lazy or unprofessional?
faq.a: Not in a subject line. It reads as a quick note, which is the goal. Keep the email body clean, with normal spelling and punctuation.

faq.q: Should the follow-ups use the same subject line?
faq.a: Most tools send follow-ups as replies in the same thread, so they keep the first subject line. That's fine. You don't need a new one for each step.

faq.q: Can I use their first name as the whole subject line?
faq.a: Yes, it's one of the most human-looking options. Just make sure the first line gives a clear reason for writing.

faq.q: How long should I test before picking a winner?
faq.a: Until each version has gone to at least 200 people and the sequence has finished. Small gaps of 1 or 2 replies are noise.
